name: Palivizumab
drug_class: Humanised monoclonal antibody against RSV fusion (F) protein
route_note: intramuscular injection once a month throughout the RSV season (usually five doses)
owner: Sobi (Swedish Orphan Biovitrum) for US rights; other regions vary

discovery.note: Humanised version of a murine antibody against a conserved epitope (site II) of the RSV F protein.

tagline: First antibody licensed against an infection, shielding high-risk babies from RSV
summary: Palivizumab is a humanised monoclonal antibody that neutralises respiratory syncytial virus by binding its F protein. Approved in 1998, it was the first monoclonal antibody licensed for an infectious disease. Given monthly during the RSV season, it reduces RSV hospitalisation in premature infants and in children with chronic lung or congenital heart disease, but it is being replaced by the single-dose nirsevimab.
mechanism: Palivizumab binds antigenic site II on the RSV fusion (F) glycoprotein, a site present on both prefusion and postfusion F. This blocks the conformational change that merges viral and cell membranes, neutralising virus and preventing cell-to-cell fusion (syncytium formation).
It is used only for prevention; it does not treat established RSV disease. Its half-life of about three weeks requires monthly dosing through the season.
uses: Prevention of serious RSV lower respiratory tract disease in children at high risk: premature infants, children with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and children with haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease

history.title: IMpact-RSV
history.detail: A trial in 1,502 high-risk infants shows about 55% reduction in RSV hospitalisation.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Synagis is approved in June 1998, the first monoclonal antibody for an infectious disease; EU approval follows in 1999.

history.title: Congenital heart disease
history.detail: Approval is extended to children with haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease.

history.title: Narrower guidance
history.detail: The American Academy of Pediatrics narrows recommendations to infants at the highest risk.

history.title: Successor
history.detail: Nirsevimab, a single-dose long-acting antibody for all infants, is approved in the US and begins to replace palivizumab.

facts: Palivizumab's high cost (thousands of dollars per season) limited its use to high-risk groups.
It was the first monoclonal antibody approved to prevent an infectious disease.
